pos: n. (the Hebrew name of the angel of the bottomless pit; named once)
etymology: Hebrew 'abaddon, destruction or the place of destruction, from 'abad, to perish or be destroyed; transliterated into Greek at Revelation 9:11 and there matched with Apollyon, the destroyer.
biblical_def: Abaddon is the Hebrew name John gives to the king over the locust-army of the fifth trumpet: “And they had a king over them, which is the angel of the bottomless pit, whose name in the Hebrew tongue is Abaddon, but in the Greek tongue hath his name Apollyon” (Revelation 9:11). The word is not a new coinage. In the Old Testament 'abaddon is one of the standing words for the realm of the dead under the aspect of ruin, set in parallel with Sheol: “Hell is naked before him, and destruction hath no covering” (Job 26:6), and again, “Hell and destruction are before the LORD: how much more then the hearts of the children of men?” (Proverbs 15:11). What the Authorized Version renders destruction in those places is this same word. John therefore does not invent a demon-name; he takes the Hebrew noun for utter ruin and makes it the proper name of the spirit who rules the pit, so that the creature is called by the thing he does. The pit itself is opened by commission and not by force: “And the fifth angel sounded, and I saw a star fall from heaven unto the earth: and to him was given the key of the bottomless pit” (Revelation 9:1). The key is given. Abaddon has a name, a kingdom, and a horde, and he has not one of them apart from the permission of God, which is the whole comfort of the passage to a reader who finds it terrible.

corruption_summary: Abaddon is treated as borrowed mythology or as a figure of speech for a mood, where Scripture names a real creature holding a real kingdom under God's permission.
corruption_paragraphs: Two errors meet over this name. The first demythologizes it: Abaddon becomes a literary personification, so that the fifth trumpet describes an inward despair rather than a spirit with a throne. The second does the opposite and makes him a rival power, a dark sovereign whose kingdom stands over against God's. Scripture allows neither. He is an angel, which is to say a creature; he is called the angel of the pit, which is to say he belongs to a place he did not make; and the key to that place is handed to another by commission (Revelation 9:1). A created destroyer with a borrowed key is neither a metaphor nor a second god.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the Authorized Version preserves the Hebrew name where a looser hand would have translated it away, and in preserving it keeps the link to Job and Proverbs, where destruction lies open and uncovered before the LORD. The pit has a king; the king has a keeper; and the hearts of the children of men are more naked before God than the pit is.

pos: n. (the land to which Sennacherib's murderers fled; the Hebrew reads Ararat)
etymology: The Authorized Version's rendering of Hebrew 'Ararat, the mountainous country north of Assyria; the translators' margin at 2 Kings 19:37 notes “Heb. Ararat.”
biblical_def: Armenia is where the sons of Sennacherib ran after they had killed their father in his own temple: “And it came to pass, as he was worshipping in the house of Nisroch his god, that Adrammelech and Sharezer his sons smote him with the sword: and they escaped into the land of Armenia” (2 Kings 19:37). Isaiah records the same end in almost the same words (Isaiah 37:38), and the repetition is the point: the prophet had said the Assyrian would not shoot an arrow into Jerusalem, and the Assyrian died by the sword of his own children in the house of his own god. The Hebrew behind Armenia is Ararat, the same word as the mountains where the ark came to rest: “And the ark rested in the seventh month, on the seventeenth day of the month, upon the mountains of Ararat” (Genesis 8:4). The translators used the name the country bore in their own day, and noted the Hebrew in the margin. The night before the flight, the siege had already been broken without a battle: “And it came to pass that night, that the angel of the LORD went out, and smote in the camp of the Assyrians an hundred fourscore and five thousand” (2 Kings 19:35). Armenia is thus a place-name that functions as a verdict. The greatest empire of the age came against Zion, and the record of its king ends with a corpse before an idol and two sons running north.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Armenia, a country of Asia; in the Authorized Version the rendering of the Hebrew Ararat.
webster_full: Armenia is the Authorized Version's name for the mountainous region north of Assyria.

corruption_summary: The Authorized Version's use of a contemporary name for an ancient region is read as an error, where the translators themselves printed the Hebrew in the margin.
corruption_paragraphs: It is sometimes urged that Armenia is a mistake, since the Hebrew says Ararat. The charge mistakes a translators' decision for ignorance. The men who set Armenia in the text are the same men who set “Heb. Ararat” in the margin beside it; they knew exactly what the Hebrew said and rendered it by the name their readers would recognize for that country. This is ordinary faithful translation, and the margin is the proof of it. A version that hides nothing in the margin is not the version to accuse of concealment.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the one the two passages were written to teach. Sennacherib had sent letters mocking the God of Israel; Hezekiah spread them before the LORD; and the answer came first as an angel in the camp and then as a sword in the temple of Nisroch. The flight into Armenia is the last line of that answer.

pos: n. (the new name given to Israel in Hosea, meaning My people; named once)
etymology: Hebrew 'ammi, my people, from 'am, a people, with the first-person suffix; the undoing of Lo-ammi, not my people, Hosea 1:9.
biblical_def: Ammi is a name of restoration, and it can only be understood against the name it reverses. Hosea was told to call his third child Lo-ammi: “Then said God, Call his name Loammi: for ye are not my people, and I will not be your God” (Hosea 1:9). That is the covenant formula taken away, and the child carried the sentence in his name wherever he went. Then comes the reversal, addressed to the next generation as a command: “Say ye unto your brethren, Ammi; and to your sisters, Ruhamah” (Hosea 2:1). The prefix of negation is struck off; not-my-people becomes My people, and not-pitied becomes Pitied. The ground of the change is not found in the people. It is announced by God in the first person: “I will sow her unto me in the earth; and I will have mercy upon her that had not obtained mercy; and I will say to them which were not my people, Thou art my people; and they shall say, Thou art my God” (Hosea 2:23). Peter takes up this very word and applies it to the church gathered out of the nations: “Which in time past were not a people, but are now the people of God: which had not obtained mercy, but now have obtained mercy” (1 Peter 2:10). Ammi is therefore one of the plainest names in Scripture for sovereign, unearned, effectual mercy — a name God gives, not one a people takes.

corruption_summary: The change from Lo-ammi to Ammi is explained as a people recovering its own identity, where Hosea makes God the only actor in the renaming.
corruption_paragraphs: The common handling of Hosea 2 turns the new name into a story about Israel's self-understanding: a community once alienated comes to see itself as belonging, and the name follows the change of outlook. The text will not carry that. Every verb in the restoration belongs to God — I will sow, I will have mercy, I will say (Hosea 2:23) — and the people's confession, “Thou art my God,” comes last, as the answer and not the cause. A name God imposes in judgment is removed the same way it was given, by the word of the One who gave it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Ammi stands as a rebuke to every attempt to make covenant membership an achievement. The same mouth that said “ye are not my people” said “Thou art my people,” and the second word is as free and as sovereign as the first was just.

pos: n. (the name given to the altar built by Reuben, Gad and half Manasseh; named once)
etymology: Hebrew 'ed, a witness; the translators' margin at Joshua 22:34 reads “that is, A witness.”
biblical_def: Ed is the shortest proper name in the Authorized Version and one of the most carefully explained. The eastern tribes, going home across Jordan, raised a great altar on the border, and the western tribes gathered for war, supposing it a rival altar and a breach of the one place of sacrifice (Joshua 22:10). The explanation they gave was that it was built never to be used: “But that it may be a witness between us, and you, and our generations after us, that we might do the service of the LORD before him with our burnt offerings, and with our sacrifices, and with our peace offerings; that your children may not say to our children in time to come, Ye have no part in the LORD” (Joshua 22:27). The naming closes the account: “And the children of Reuben and the children of Gad called the altar Ed: for it shall be a witness between us that the LORD is God” (Joshua 22:34). The practice is old in Israel; Laban had done the same with a heap of stones: “And Laban said, This heap is a witness between me and thee this day. Therefore was the name of it called Galeed” (Genesis 31:48). What makes Ed remarkable is the restraint. An altar that offers nothing is the one kind of altar the law permitted beside the tabernacle, and the tribes were willing to be suspected of schism rather than let the generations forget that Jordan is not a covenant boundary.

corruption_summary: Joshua 22 is read as a quarrel over territory, where the dispute is about the unity of worship and the altar is named to settle it.
corruption_paragraphs: The episode is often told as tribal politics, with the altar a flag and the near-war a border incident. The chapter itself is about worship. The western tribes feared a second place of sacrifice, which the law forbade, and they said so; the eastern tribes answered that the structure would never see a sacrifice, and named it accordingly. That the whole nation was ready to go to war over an unauthorized altar, and that the misunderstanding was cleared by a plain account of what the thing was for, is a standing testimony to how seriously Israel once took the regulative principle of worship.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is twofold: that nothing may be added to the worship God has commanded, however pious the motive; and that brethren under suspicion owe one another a plain explanation before the sword is drawn. Ed was built to speak to children not yet born, and what it says is, “the LORD is God.”

pos: n. (named twice in Jeremiah as the father of Jerahmeel and of Malchiah)
etymology: Hebrew ham-melek, literally the king, the noun melek with the definite article; carried into the Authorized Version as a proper name at Jeremiah 36:26 and 38:6.
biblical_def: Hammelech appears twice, each time as the father of a man employed against Jeremiah. The first is in the account of the burned roll: “But the king commanded Jerahmeel the son of Hammelech, and Seraiah the son of Azriel, and Shelemiah the son of Abdeel, to take Baruch the scribe and Jeremiah the prophet: but the LORD hid them” (Jeremiah 36:26). The second names the pit into which the prophet was lowered: “Then took they Jeremiah, and cast him into the dungeon of Malchiah the son of Hammelech, that was in the court of the prison” (Jeremiah 38:6). The Hebrew is the king with the article, so that the phrase may be read either as a name or as a description, the king's son; the Authorized Version keeps it as a name and lets the reader weigh it. Either way the men so described are of the royal house or household, and both times they are set to work against the word of God. The setting is Jehoiakim at the hearth: “And it came to pass, that when Jehudi had read three or four leaves, he cut it with the penknife, and cast it into the fire that was on the hearth, until all the roll was consumed in the fire that was on the hearth” (Jeremiah 36:23). The answer to that penknife is the last verse of the chapter: “Then took Jeremiah another roll, and gave it to Baruch the scribe, the son of Neriah; who wrote therein from the mouth of Jeremiah all the words of the book which Jehoiakim king of Judah had burned in the fire: and there were added besides unto them many like words” (Jeremiah 36:32).

corruption_summary: The burning of the roll is treated as the suppression of a text, where Jeremiah 36 is written to show that the word cannot be destroyed.
corruption_paragraphs: Jehoiakim's penknife is a favourite image for the power of rulers over Scripture, and it is read as a story about censorship succeeding. The chapter is composed to say the reverse. The roll was burned leaf by leaf; the prophet dictated it again; and the second roll was longer than the first, for “there were added besides unto them many like words” (Jeremiah 36:32). The officers sent to arrest the writers found no one, because “the LORD hid them” (Jeremiah 36:26). A king with a fire and a court full of servants was the weaker party.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the providential preservation of Scripture, which is not an abstraction but a history of burned rolls, flooded presses and executed translators, with the text still in our hands. Hammelech's sons stand in that history on the losing side, and the dungeon of Malchiah held the prophet for a time but not the prophecy.

pos: n. (the name Ezekiel gives to the high place of Israel's idolatry; named once)
etymology: Hebrew bamah, a high place or elevation; the ordinary word for the hill-shrines of Canaanite and apostate Israelite worship, used once at Ezekiel 20:29 as a proper name.
biblical_def: Bamah is the common Hebrew noun for a high place, turned into a name by way of rebuke: “Then I said unto them, What is the high place whereunto ye go? And the name thereof is called Bamah unto this day” (Ezekiel 20:29). The question is contemptuous. God has been reciting the history of Israel's rebellions, and when He reaches the shrines on the hills He asks what the thing even is, and then says that its name is simply High Place — as if to say the whole apparatus has no more content than the hill it stands on. The charge immediately before explains it: “For when I had brought them into the land, for the which I lifted up mine hand to give it to them, then they saw every high hill, and all the thick trees, and they offered there their sacrifices” (Ezekiel 20:28). The sin is not that they stopped sacrificing but that they chose their own places to do it. The law had promised the end of these shrines from the beginning: “And I will destroy your high places, and cut down your images, and cast your carcases upon the carcases of your idols, and my soul shall abhor you” (Leviticus 26:30), and the faithful kings carried it out: “He removed the high places, and brake the images, and cut down the groves” (2 Kings 18:4). Bamah is the name of will-worship exposed by being named plainly.

corruption_summary: The high places are excused as sincere local devotion to the true God, where Scripture names them as self-chosen worship and condemns them as such.
corruption_paragraphs: A familiar reading makes the high places a harmless folk piety: the people meant to worship the LORD, only nearer home, and the prophets were severe about a matter of arrangement. Ezekiel 20 answers that the arrangement was the sin. They saw every high hill and the thick trees and offered there (Ezekiel 20:28) — the choice was made by the eye, and the worship followed the scenery. Worship that God has not commanded is not a lesser obedience; it is will-worship, and the Scripture treats it as provocation, not as enthusiasm needing better direction.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the regulative principle: what God commands in His worship is required, and what He has not commanded is not permitted. Bamah is what a self-chosen shrine is called when God names it, and the name is a bare noun, because there was nothing else in it to name.

pos: adj. (of Babylon; used once, of the garment Achan coveted)
etymology: From Babylon, with the English adjectival ending -ish; the Authorized Version's rendering of the Hebrew phrase for a robe of Shinar, Joshua 7:21.
biblical_def: Babylonish occurs once, in Achan's confession: “When I saw among the spoils a goodly Babylonish garment, and two hundred shekels of silver, and a wedge of gold of fifty shekels weight, then I coveted them, and took them; and, behold, they are hid in the earth in the midst of my tent, and the silver under it” (Joshua 7:21). The Hebrew calls it a robe of Shinar, and the translators rendered it by the adjective their readers would understand. The order of the verbs in that sentence is the anatomy of every sin of covetousness: he saw, he coveted, he took, he hid. Jericho had been devoted whole to the LORD, so that every thread of it was holy to Him, and one man's tent-floor made the whole army liable: “But the children of Israel committed a trespass in the accursed thing: for Achan, the son of Carmi, the son of Zabdi, the son of Zerah, of the tribe of Judah, took of the accursed thing: and the anger of the LORD was kindled against the children of Israel” (Joshua 7:1). The judgment fell in the valley of Achor: “And Joshua said, Why hast thou troubled us? the LORD shall trouble thee this day. And all Israel stoned him with stones” (Joshua 7:25). The apostle names the root exactly: “covetousness, which is idolatry” (Colossians 3:5). A fine foreign robe no one would ever wear, buried under a tent, cost thirty-six men their lives at Ai.

corruption_summary: Achan's judgment is called disproportionate, where Scripture presents his theft as sacrilege and his sentence as the vindication of what was devoted to God.
corruption_paragraphs: The usual complaint against Joshua 7 is arithmetic: a garment, some silver, a wedge of gold, and a man and his household destroyed. The complaint misses what the devoted thing was. Jericho was the firstfruits of the land, given whole to the LORD, so that taking from it was not theft from the army but sacrilege against God — the same category as Ananias keeping back part of the price. The text is also careful to show that the nation was not punished for one man's sin without cause: the trespass was Israel's (Joshua 7:1), because Israel was one body and the accursed thing was in the camp.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the exact sequence Achan confessed: I saw, I coveted, I took, I hid. Covetousness is named idolatry by the apostle (Colossians 3:5) because it seats a thing where God should sit, and the proof of it here is that the robe was never worn, never sold, never used — only buried, and kept.

pos: adj. (of Canaan; used twice, of the mother of Shaul son of Simeon)
etymology: From Canaanite, with the English adjectival ending -ish; used in the Authorized Version only of the woman who bore Shaul to Simeon, Genesis 46:10 and Exodus 6:15.
biblical_def: Canaanitish occurs twice, and both times in the same genealogical note: “And the sons of Simeon; Jemuel, and Jamin, and Ohad, and Jachin, and Zohar, and Shaul the son of a Canaanitish woman” (Genesis 46:10), repeated at Exodus 6:15. The detail is not decoration. Among all the sons of Jacob's sons whose names are simply listed, one has his mother's nation recorded, and it is the nation marked for judgment and specifically excluded from marriage with the covenant line. Abraham had bound his servant by oath on that very point: “And I will make thee swear by the LORD, the God of heaven, and the God of the earth, that thou shalt not take a wife unto my son of the daughters of the Canaanites, among whom I dwell” (Genesis 24:3). The law afterwards made it a standing command: “Neither shalt thou make marriages with them; thy daughter thou shalt not give unto his son, nor his daughter shalt thou take unto thy son” (Deuteronomy 7:3). Scripture records the marriage without comment and leaves the single adjective to do the work, as it does with Judah and Tamar, and with Samson. The honesty of the register is itself a doctrine: the genealogies of the covenant people are not cleaned up, and the line through which Christ came is reported with its irregularities intact.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Canaanitish, pertaining to Canaan or its inhabitants; used in Scripture of the mother of Shaul, son of Simeon.
webster_full: Canaanitish is an adjective meaning pertaining to Canaan.
It occurs twice in the Authorized Version, Genesis 46:10 and Exodus 6:15.
Both places describe the mother of Shaul, a son of Simeon.
Marriage with the Canaanites was forbidden to the covenant line.
The note is recorded plainly and without comment.
scriptures: And the sons of Simeon; Jemuel, and Jamin, and Ohad, and Jachin, and Zohar, and Shaul the son of a Canaanitish woman.
Exo 6:15
And the sons of Simeon; Jemuel, and Jamin, and Ohad, and Jachin, and Zohar, and Shaul the son of a Canaanitish woman: these are the families of Simeon.
Gen 24:3
And I will make thee swear by the LORD, the God of heaven, and the God of the earth, that thou shalt not take a wife unto my son of the daughters of the Canaanites, among whom I dwell:
Deu 7:3
Neither shalt thou make marriages with them; thy daughter thou shalt not give unto his son, nor his daughter shalt thou take unto thy son.
corruption_summary: The prohibition of Canaanite marriage is read as ethnic exclusion, where Scripture grounds it in religion and admits Canaanites who come to faith.
corruption_paragraphs: The command of Deuteronomy 7:3 is regularly produced as evidence that Scripture teaches a racial purity, and the single word Canaanitish is read as a slur on a woman's blood. The ground given in the text is not blood but worship: the daughters would turn the sons away to serve other gods, and that is the reason stated in the next verse. Scripture proves the point by the exceptions it honours — Rahab of Jericho and Ruth the Moabitess both enter the line of Christ, and neither changed her ancestry. What changed was the God she confessed.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the unequal yoke, which stands in the New Testament as firmly as in the Old and on the same religious ground, together with the plain honesty of the biblical genealogies. The register notes the Canaanitish mother, and the same register runs on to Christ.
roots_summary: English adjective from Canaanite; Genesis 46:10, Exodus 6:15.
roots_lines: From Canaanite with the adjectival ending -ish.
Used twice in the Authorized Version, of one woman.
She was the mother of Shaul, a son of Simeon.
Marriage with Canaanites was forbidden on religious grounds.
Compare Rahab and Ruth, received into the covenant by faith.

pos: n. (a woman of Carmel; used of Abigail, formerly Nabal's wife)
etymology: The feminine of Carmelite, a native of Carmel in Judah; used in the Authorized Version of Abigail, 1 Samuel 27:3 and 1 Chronicles 3:1.
biblical_def: Carmelitess is the feminine gentilic the Authorized Version gives Abigail after her first husband's death: “And David dwelt with Achish at Gath, he and his men, every man with his household, even David with his two wives, Ahinoam the Jezreelitess, and Abigail the Carmelitess, Nabal's wife” (1 Samuel 27:3). The form is rare, and the English keeps the feminine ending that the Hebrew also marks. Carmel here is not the mountain of Elijah's contest but the town in the hill country of Judah where Nabal had his sheep. Her character is set out plainly when she is introduced: “Now the name of the man was Nabal; and the name of his wife Abigail: and she was a woman of good understanding, and of a beautiful countenance: but the man was churlish and evil in his doings; and he was of the house of Caleb” (1 Samuel 25:3). She intercepted David on the road with provisions and with an argument, and kept him from avenging himself; and when Nabal died she came at David's word: “And Abigail hasted, and arose, and rode upon an ass, with five damsels of hers that went after her; and she went after the messengers of David, and became his wife” (1 Samuel 25:42). She shared his exile and his losses, taken captive with Ahinoam when the Amalekites burned Ziklag (1 Samuel 30:5). The title marks a woman of discretion who is named by her town and remembered for her wisdom.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Carmelitess, a woman of Carmel; used in Scripture of Abigail, the wife of Nabal and afterward of David.
webster_full: Carmelitess is the feminine form of Carmelite, a native of Carmel.
The Carmel intended is the town in the hill country of Judah.
It is used of Abigail, 1 Samuel 27:3 and 1 Chronicles 3:1.
She was first the wife of Nabal and afterward of David.
The Hebrew likewise marks the feminine ending.
scriptures: And David dwelt with Achish at Gath, he and his men, every man with his household, even David with his two wives, Ahinoam the Jezreelitess, and Abigail the Carmelitess, Nabal's wife.

Now the name of the man was Nabal; and the name of his wife Abigail: and she was a woman of good understanding, and of a beautiful countenance: but the man was churlish and evil in his doings; and he was of the house of Caleb.
And Abigail hasted, and arose, and rode upon an ass, with five damsels of hers that went after her; and she went after the messengers of David, and became his wife.
And David's two wives were taken captives, Ahinoam the Jezreelitess, and Abigail the wife of Nabal the Carmelite.
corruption_summary: Abigail is enlisted either to overturn the creational order of the home or to teach that a wife must assist her husband's folly; Scripture commends her for doing neither.
corruption_paragraphs: Abigail is pressed into service by two opposite errors. One makes her a case against the headship of husbands, as though her independent action proved the order itself defective; the other makes submission mean compliance in sin, so that she should have let Nabal's insult stand and the household perish with him. Scripture commends her without granting either. She acted to save lives from a sin not her own, and her first words to David are an appeal to the LORD and to David's own calling, not an assertion of her rights. A wife's submission is to the Lord first, and that is why her obedience to God in a crisis is not a breach of her place but the proof of it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the one she herself urged: that vengeance belongs to the LORD, and that a man who will one day be king must not come to the throne with innocent blood on his hands. David blessed God for her advice, and the Authorized Version keeps her town in her name.

pos: n. pl. (a people over whom Abner made Ish-bosheth king; named twice)
etymology: A gentilic plural; at 2 Samuel 2:9 one of the territories of Ish-bosheth's short reign, and at Ezekiel 27:6 a company whose work is named among the furnishings of Tyre.
biblical_def: The Ashurites are named twice. The first is in the list of what Abner secured for Saul's surviving son: “And made him king over Gilead, and over the Ashurites, and over Jezreel, and over Ephraim, and over Benjamin, and over all Israel” (2 Samuel 2:9). The list is impressive and the reality was not. The next verse gives the measure of it: “Ishbosheth Saul's son was forty years old when he began to reign over Israel, and reigned two years. But the house of Judah followed David” (2 Samuel 2:10). Meanwhile the tribe that mattered had already acted: “And the men of Judah came, and there they anointed David king over the house of Judah” (2 Samuel 2:4). The second occurrence stands among the ship-furnishings of Tyre: “Of the oaks of Bashan have they made thine oars; the company of the Ashurites have made thy benches of ivory, brought out of the isles of Chittim” (Ezekiel 27:6). Whether the same people are meant in both places the text does not say, and the dictionary will not pretend to more than Scripture gives. What the first passage gives plainly is the shape of a rival kingdom: a general, a puppet, a long list of provinces, and two years. The true succession was settled elsewhere: “In Hebron he reigned over Judah seven years and six months: and in Jerusalem he reigned thirty and three years over all Israel and Judah” (2 Samuel 5:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Ashurites, a people named in the reign of Ish-bosheth and again among the craftsmen of Tyre.
webster_full: Ashurites is a gentilic plural occurring twice in the Authorized Version.
At 2 Samuel 2:9 they are a territory of Ish-bosheth's brief kingdom.
At Ezekiel 27:6 a company of Ashurites works ivory benches for Tyre.
Scripture does not state whether one people is meant in both places.
The name is distinct from Asshur, the founder of Assyria.
scriptures: And made him king over Gilead, and over the Ashurites, and over Jezreel, and over Ephraim, and over Benjamin, and over all Israel.
Ishbosheth Saul's son was forty years old when he began to reign over Israel, and reigned two years. But the house of Judah followed David.
And the men of Judah came, and there they anointed David king over the house of Judah. And they told David, saying, That the men of Jabeshgilead were they that buried Saul.
In Hebron he reigned over Judah seven years and six months: and in Jerusalem he reigned thirty and three years over all Israel and Judah.
corruption_summary: Obscure names like this are treated as proof that the text is confused; the honest answer is that Scripture says less here than we would like and no more than is true.
corruption_paragraphs: Two opposite temptations attend a word like Ashurites. The first is the critical one, which takes a name used twice in unrelated settings as evidence of a corrupt or composite text. The second is the harmonizing one, which invents a history to tie the two verses together and presents the invention as knowledge. Neither is faithful. The Authorized Version renders what the Hebrew has; the reader may note that the identification is not given and leave it there. A reference work that marks the limits of revelation is more trustworthy than one that fills them.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the one 2 Samuel 2 presses by its arithmetic. Abner could name six territories and crown a king over them, and it came to two years, because the kingdom had been promised elsewhere. Lists of provinces are not the same as a throne, and the house of Judah followed David.

roots_lines: A gentilic plural of uncertain identification.
Named at 2 Samuel 2:9 among the realms of Ish-bosheth.

Not to be confused with Asshur or with Assyria.
Abner set Ish-bosheth over them, and he reigned two years.
